tasks.short: Develop the safeguard plan for computer files

steps.what: Submit computer files and emergency processing hours
Match files against destruction and disclosure
Draft a safeguard against accidental modification

loop.input: file class, threat and emergency hours
loop.output: draft section tagged to those fields
loop.check: Each threat is modification, destruction or disclosure from the form
loop.stop: Leave the section blank and stop if emergency hours have no field
loop.why_not_simpler: Emergency prose differs by system and a fixed merge cannot write it

steps.what: Sign the safeguard against unauthorized disclosure
File the signed safeguard plan

tasks.design: Service owners submit system id, file class, threat and emergency hours on a {WORKFLOW} form. A bounded draft in {DOCS} writes a safeguard section only where those fields exist. The security analyst signs that version, and only then does {DOCS} file it. No control is switched on from the plan.
tasks.previous_blocker: Safeguard text was recopied from old documents, and emergency hours lived in mail, so a draft would have repeated stale targets.
tasks.enabler_now: The file inventory and the form can share one system id, so each threat and hour in the draft can be checked against a field.
tasks.still_hard: Deciding which disclosure risk is acceptable, and which emergency processing path the business can live with, is still a judgement.
tasks.human_edge: The analyst decides which accidental or unauthorized cases the plan accepts, and which emergency hours are real.

ambition.what: Re-sign the safeguard plan when a file class is added, not only at the yearly review

tasks.altitude: The week moves from rewriting sections to closing gaps and signing. The analyst can refuse a plan whose threats do not match the form.

reach.task: Keep emergency processing inside the signed hours
reach.learn: Which file classes are signed and which emergency hours are still blank

evidence.claim: In a mid-size firm this task is a document plus a review. The hard part is which files need which safeguard, not the formatting.
Digest [S16] and [S18] say Dutch cyber law has been in force since 15 August 2026 and includes a duty of care. Sector and size decide whether a firm is in scope.
Digest [S19] says firms in scope report incidents at 24 hours, 72 hours and one month. This plan names who would report. It does not file the notice.
Digest [S28] reports a coding agent that deleted a production database despite instructions, so this task files a signed plan and does not apply controls on its own.

assumptions: Focal role is the security analyst. The task ends when a signed safeguard plan is filed. Switching on a control is a later task.

Input contract: system id, file class, threat (modification, destruction or disclosure), emergency processing hours, business owner. Producer is the service owner. If the form is empty the analyst types the same fields and marks the row manual.
Use the document store's own templates and approval flow before custom code. Template upkeep is counted in incremental hours.
unknowns: Whether this firm is in scope of the Dutch cyber duty of care.
Which system is the file inventory of record.
Who may sign when the analyst is absent.
research_questions: What share of file classes has no emergency hours?
How often does a signed threat differ from the last incident?

already_counted.description: Analyst rewrites weak emergency sections in the draft
Analyst time on disclosure choices in the sign-off

incremental.description: Update the plan template when a new file class appears
Service owners correct stale emergency hours the form rejects

approvals.approved_version: safeguard plan version signed in this review
the same signed safeguard plan version

time_saved_range_pct.basis: The low case assumes half the file classes still arrive as free-text mail, so the analyst retypes threats and hours. The high case assumes the form is used but every plan still has a full sign-off. Applying controls is not treated as saved.

tasks.savings_basis: 100 focal-role baseline hours; external labour excluded; incremental focal work deducted once; provisional

tasks.short: Monitor reports of viruses and update protection

steps.what: Read current reports of computer viruses
Match viruses to protection systems

loop.input: bulletin id and product id on each report row
loop.output: protection systems behind a named bulletin
loop.check: Every cited product id is on the protection inventory
loop.stop: One pass; a row with no product id stays on the manual list
loop.why_not_simpler: Bulletin wording does not map to a product id by a fixed table

steps.what: Decide when protection systems should update
Apply the signed protection update
Record which systems stayed unchanged

tasks.design: Virus reports land as rows on the {DATA_PLATFORM} with a bulletin id and a product id. A bounded pass matches them to protection systems in the {OPS_SYSTEM}. The analyst decides the update. The {OPS_SYSTEM} applies it only for that signed decision, never on its own.
tasks.previous_blocker: Bulletins arrived as unstructured mail and notes, so a feed could not tell which protection system a report referred to.
tasks.enabler_now: A report can carry a bulletin id and a product id that the protection inventory already uses.
tasks.still_hard: Whether to update during the working day, when a definition might disrupt a system, is still a judgement.
tasks.human_edge: The analyst decides when protection systems should update, and refuses a bulletin that names no product.

ambition.what: Decide virus updates on the day the report arrives, not in a monthly batch

tasks.altitude: Less time collecting bulletins, more time on the update decision. The analyst can block an update that has no signed decision.

reach.task: Roll back a protection update the analyst stopped
reach.learn: Which product ids were updated and which were left unchanged

evidence.claim: Reading virus bulletins and deciding on a definition update is routine console work in a mid-size firm. The decision is not a threshold.
Digest [S7] and [S8] describe a managed detection service for mid-size firms that uses models to speed investigation, while the analysts still decide.
Digest [S13] reports an observational study of live security operations with shorter resolve times after a generative assistant versus matched peers. It was not a randomised trial.
Digest [S16] and [S18] say Dutch cyber law has been in force since 15 August 2026 and the duty of care includes patching for firms in scope. Scope depends on sector and size.
Digest [S28] reports a coding agent that deleted a production database despite instructions, so no agent changes a virus-protection setting by itself.

assumptions: Focal role is the security analyst. The task runs from a virus report to a signed update or a row left unchanged. Definition intake is not a view of named staff.
Input contract: bulletin id, product id, severity, published time, protection system id. Producer is the report feed. If the product id is missing the row stays on a manual list and is not updated.
Use the protection console's own update job before custom code. The meeting share in the prior does not fit this task: time today is on bulletin documents and the console.
unknowns: Whether production definition updates are frozen outside a change window.
Which protection systems have no job interface.
Whether this firm is in scope of the cyber duty of care.
research_questions: What share of virus reports arrives with no product id?
How often is the first definition update rolled back?

already_counted.description: Analyst still reads weak bulletin matches
Analyst decision time on whether to update

incremental.description: Add product ids when a new protection system is installed

approvals.approved_version: protection update decision for this bulletin set
the same signed protection update decision

time_saved_range_pct.basis: The low case assumes most bulletins stay free text, so the match rarely fires and the analyst still reads them. The high case assumes clean ids but every update decision stays with the analyst. Rollback work is not treated as saved.

tasks.savings_basis: 100 focal-role baseline hours; external labour excluded; incremental focal work deducted once; provisional

steps.what: Read tainted digital transfers
Draft firewalls for confidential transmissions

loop.input: path id, encryption state and tainted-transfer flag
loop.output: rule note that cites path ids only
loop.check: Every cited path id is on the path gap list
loop.stop: Stop after one draft and drop any sentence with no path id
loop.why_not_simpler: Why a path should be encrypted is not a fixed lookup

steps.what: Sign the encrypt rule for these firewalls
Apply only the signed firewalls
Erect remaining firewalls by hand

tasks.design: Path id, encryption state and a tainted-transfer flag come from the {OPS_SYSTEM}. A bounded note in {DOCS} cites only those path ids. The security analyst signs the firewall version. The {OPS_SYSTEM} applies that version. Paths with no rule id are erected by hand.
tasks.previous_blocker: Encryption gaps and firewall exceptions were spread across consoles and meeting notes, so a change could not show which path it relied on.
tasks.enabler_now: Each transmission path can be exported with a path id, an encryption state and a tainted-transfer flag.
tasks.still_hard: Whether a path may stay open is a business trade-off, and some appliances still have no job interface.
tasks.human_edge: The analyst signs the encrypt and firewall version, and erects by hand any path the rule cannot name.

ambition.what: Review open firewall exceptions every month instead of only after an incident

tasks.altitude: Known paths take less gathering. The analyst keeps the right to refuse a live firewall or encrypt change.

reach.task: Retire a firewall exception the analyst marked expired
reach.learn: Which path ids are signed and which are still erected by hand

evidence.claim: In a mid-size firm, encrypting a path and changing a firewall are console work. Only paths with a stable rule id suit a job. The rest stay manual.
Digest [S22] says security logging must stay necessary and proportionate. A transmission log should record path id and result, not message contents.
Digest [S16] and [S18] say Dutch cyber law has been in force since 15 August 2026 and includes a duty of care for firms in scope. Scope depends on sector and size.
Digest [S28] reports a coding agent that deleted a production database despite instructions, so no agent changes a firewall or an encrypt setting by itself.

assumptions: Focal role is the security analyst. A production firewall or encrypt change runs only after a signed rule version. Uncoded paths stay on the hand queue.
Input contract: path id, encryption state, tainted-transfer flag, rule id, owner. Producer is the operations export. If the rule id is missing the path is not applied by the job.
Use the firewall console's own rule job before custom code. Logging of transmissions stays limited to security events, not a view of named people.
unknowns: Whether production rule changes are frozen outside a change window.
Which appliances have no job interface.
Whether this firm is in scope of the cyber duty of care.
research_questions: What share of paths has no rule id?
How many firewall exceptions have no owner or no expiry?

already_counted.description: Analyst edits the rule note before signing
Hands-on erect time stays with the analyst

incremental.description: Add rule ids when a new path type appears

approvals.approved_version: firewall rule version signed for these path ids
the same signed firewall rule version
hand erect decision for paths with no rule id

time_saved_range_pct.basis: The low case assumes most paths have no rule id, so the analyst still erects firewalls by hand. The high case assumes coded paths apply after a signature, while every exception and every hand change stays with the analyst. No unattended changes.

tasks.savings_basis: 100 focal-role baseline hours; external labour excluded; incremental focal work deducted once; provisional

tasks.short: Test processing systems and security measures

steps.what: Open last tests of the processing system
Draft risk assessments from control rows

loop.input: control id, system id and last test result
loop.output: assessment rows that cite control ids
loop.check: Every cited control id is on the control test list
loop.stop: One pass; a row with no control id is left blank
loop.why_not_simpler: The risk narrative is not a fixed lookup from the last result

steps.what: Choose the tests to execute
Run signed checks of security measures
Judge functioning of processing activities

tasks.design: Control id, system id and last test result sit on the {DATA_PLATFORM}. A bounded sheet in {DOCS} cites those ids. The analyst chooses which tests to execute. Read-only checks run on the {OPS_SYSTEM} only for that choice. The analyst judges whether security measures functioned.
tasks.previous_blocker: Test evidence was a mix of screenshots and free-text notes, so a sheet could not show which control a result belonged to.
tasks.enabler_now: Controls can be exported as rows with a control id, a system id and a last result.
tasks.still_hard: A failed check is not by itself a judgement that the activity is unsafe, and a live test must not change the system.
tasks.human_edge: The analyst chooses the tests to execute and judges whether the measures are functioning.

ambition.what: Execute the functioning tests every month, not only before the yearly audit

tasks.altitude: Less time assembling old results, more time on which tests to run and what a failure means. The analyst can stop a check that is not read-only.

reach.task: Rerun a read-only check the analyst marked failed
reach.learn: Which control ids were in the signed test set and which failures are still open

evidence.claim: Risk tests in a mid-size firm are a control list, a run, and a person reading the result. Novel failures do not map to a fixed pass rule.
Digest [S14] says a vendor pentest agent closed a minority of reports, and many others were duplicates or informative, so a person still reads the finding before a test is treated as closed.
Digest [S16] and [S18] say Dutch cyber law has been in force since 15 August 2026 and includes a duty of care for firms in scope. Scope depends on sector and size.
Digest [S19] says firms in scope report incidents at 24 hours, 72 hours and one month. A failed test is not itself that notice.
Digest [S28] reports a coding agent that deleted a production database despite instructions, so tests that would change a live system do not run unattended.

assumptions: Focal role is the security analyst. The task ends at a judged test record. Filing an incident notice is a separate task.
Input contract: control id, system id, last test result, last test date, measure id. Producer is the control export. Rows with no control id are not executed.
Use the operations console's own read-only check before custom code. Checks that write or restart a system stay on the manual queue.
unknowns: Whether this firm is in scope of the cyber duty of care.
Which checks are read-only versus live changes.
Who may sign a test set when the analyst is absent.
research_questions: What share of controls has no test in the last quarter?
How many failed checks were duplicates of an older finding?

already_counted.description: Analyst edits assessment rows the sheet got wrong
Analyst judgement on whether measures functioned

incremental.description: Add control ids when a new processing system is in scope

approvals.approved_version: test set signed for this system id

time_saved_range_pct.basis: The low case assumes most controls have no stable id, so the sheet stays empty and the analyst still assembles tests by hand. The high case assumes coded checks run after a signature, while every failure is still judged by the analyst. Incident notices are not treated as saved.

tasks.savings_basis: 100 focal-role baseline hours; external labour excluded; incremental focal work deducted once; provisional

role.altitude: The analyst stops retyping safeguard text and virus bulletins, and spends the week on disclosure choices, update decisions, firewall versions and which tests to run.
reach: Network operators receive the signed safeguard plan and the test set, and do not apply a firewall or a protection update that lacks that version.
Service owners see which file classes still have no emergency hours.
skills_to_grow: Write a safeguard plan as fields a template can check.
State a virus update as a bulletin id, a product id and a decision.
Separate a signed firewall rule from a path that still needs a hand change.
Choose a test set that cites control ids before any check runs.
role.ambitious_version: Every file class has a signed safeguard plan, virus updates wait for a decision, and firewall or test changes run only from a signed version.
